paper_context.research_question: How do two classes of evaluation metrics—prerequisite skills (cognitive/inference skills) and readability (lexical/syntactic complexity)—characterize existing reading comprehension (RC) datasets, and how are question difficulty (as proxied by required prerequisite skills) and text readability related?
contribution_style: empirical evaluation across multiple existing datasets
methodological: specification of metrics and annotation protocol
descriptive/analytical: comparative characterization and correlation analysis
main_claims: A refined taxonomy of 13 prerequisite skills (building on prior work) can be used to annotate RC questions and characterize question difficulty.
Readability metrics (lexical, syntactic, traditional indices) and prerequisite-skill annotations together provide complementary views of dataset quality.

Across six analyzed RC datasets (QA4MRE, MCTest, SQuAD, Who-did-What, MS MARCO, NewsQA) there is only a weak correlation between text readability and number of prerequisite skills required to answer questions.
It is possible to produce datasets (e.g., MCTest) that are easy to read but contain difficult questions, and conversely datasets that are hard to read but easy to answer (e.g., SQuAD).
Annotated labels and the two-metric framework can guide dataset construction and system development (e.g., curriculum learning stages).
expected_evaluation_dimensions: Annotation reliability: inter-annotator agreement on prerequisite-skill labels and nonsense/solvable judgments
Coverage and granularity of the prerequisite-skill taxonomy (does it capture phenomena needed across diverse datasets?)
Validity of the skill-count proxy for question difficulty (does number of skills correlate with system/human performance?)
Appropriateness and sensitivity of chosen readability features for modeling reading difficulty in RC contexts
Statistical analysis robustness: sampling method (100 questions per dataset), correlation measures, and significance testing
Generality: applicability of the annotation procedure across different RC formulations (span, multiple-choice, cloze, multi-segment)
Resource utility: clarity, format, and accessibility of the released annotations for reuse

extracted_claims.claim_text: A refined taxonomy of 13 prerequisite skills (reorganizing and extending prior work) can be used to annotate RC questions and characterize question difficulty.
evidence: Section 3.1 lists and defines 13 prerequisite skills (Object tracking, Mathematical reasoning, Coreference resolution, Logical reasoning, Analogy, Causal relation, Spatiotemporal relation, Ellipsis, Bridging, Elaboration, Meta-knowledge, Schematic clause relation, Punctuation).
Introduction contribution 2: 'We revise the previous classification of prerequisite skills for RC.'
Annotation procedure (4.1) applied these skills to six datasets.

No detailed per-skill agreement or confusion matrix provided in main text.
Taxonomy design choices (why these 13 and not others) are partly motivated by theoretical sources but some labeling boundaries (e.g., bridging vs elaboration) may be subjective.

extracted_claims.claim_label: Skill-count as proxy for question difficulty
extracted_claims.claim_text: The number of required prerequisite skills corresponds to the difficulty of an RC question (i.e., more skills required → more difficult).
extracted_claims.section_anchor: Introduction; Section 3.1 (paragraphs referencing Sugawara et al. and assumption)
evidence: Introduction: 'From this observation, we assume that the number of required skills corresponds to the difficulty of a question.'
Reference to Sugawara et al. (2017) which observed that more skills required relate to higher difficulty.
uncertainty_flags: No direct validation in this paper linking skill-count to system or human performance on the same questions (expected evaluation dimension noted but not resolved).
Assumes independence and equal weight of skills; no weighting or interaction model reported.
Potential confound: some labeled skills may reflect annotation choices rather than intrinsic difficulty.

extracted_claims.claim_text: Readability metrics (lexical, syntactic, traditional indices) and prerequisite-skill annotations together provide complementary views of dataset quality.
extracted_claims.section_anchor: Abstract; Section 3 and 5 (readability metrics and dataset analysis)

Section 5 compares readability results (Table 4 referenced) and skill annotations (Tables 2–3) across datasets and discusses different patterns (e.g., SQuAD hard to read but easy to answer).

Readability metrics are originally designed for human readers; their relevance to system performance is acknowledged as uncertain.

extracted_claims.claim_label: Weak correlation between readability and skill-count
extracted_claims.claim_text: Across six analyzed RC datasets (QA4MRE, MCTest, SQuAD, Who-did-What, MS MARCO, NewsQA) there is only a weak correlation between text readability (e.g., Flesch–Kincaid) and number of prerequisite skills required to answer questions.
extracted_claims.section_anchor: Section 5 (iv) Correlation between numbers of required prerequisite skills and readability metrics; Figures 3–4; Table 5
evidence: Section 5: 'Although there are weak correlations from 0.025 to 0.416, the results highlight that there is not necessarily a strong correlation between the two values.'
Figures 3 and 4 show plots of Flesch–Kincaid grade levels versus average/individual question skill counts; Table 5 reports Pearson correlations (values referenced).
uncertainty_flags: Correlation coefficients range up to 0.416 — described as weak but magnitude and significance per metric/dataset not fully elaborated in text.
Sampling: only 100 randomly sampled questions per dataset; representativeness unclear, especially for large heterogeneous datasets.
Pearson correlation assumes linear relationship; potential non-linear patterns not explored.

extracted_claims.claim_text: It is possible to produce datasets that are easy to read but contain difficult questions (e.g., MCTest), and conversely datasets that are hard to read but easy to answer (e.g., SQuAD).

uncertainty_flags: Designation 'difficult to answer' is based on skill-count proxy rather than direct performance metrics; without that link the conclusion is indirect.
MCTest sample and SQuAD sample selection protocols may influence observed patterns (e.g., paragraph selection in SQuAD sampling).

extracted_claims.claim_text: Annotated labels and the two-metric framework can guide dataset construction and system development (e.g., curriculum learning stages); annotations for six datasets are made publicly available.

extracted_claims.claim_label: Annotation procedure equivalence across task formulations
extracted_claims.claim_text: The annotation protocol (select sentences needed to answer, then label prerequisite skills) is equivalent across different RC task formulations (span, multiple-choice, cloze, multi-segment) for evaluating contextual entailments.
extracted_claims.section_anchor: End of Introduction; Section 4.1 Annotation Procedure
evidence: Introduction: 'In the annotation, annotators selected sentences needed for answering and then annotated them with prerequisite skills under the same condition for RC datasets with different task formulations.'
Section 4.1 describes showing context, question, and answer jointly to annotators for all tasks and marking sentences and skills.
uncertainty_flags: Authors note limitation: methodology 'could not evaluate the competence of looking for sentences that need to be read and answer candidates' — i.e., selection equivalence assumption has limits.
Different dataset formats may constrain what annotators can mark (e.g., aggregated segments in MS MARCO), potential variation in annotation fidelity across formats not quantified.

extracted_claims.claim_text: Inter-annotator agreement on the prerequisite-skill annotation is 90.1% on a 62-question random sample.

identified_assumptions.assumption_text: Number of prerequisite skills required (skill-count) is a valid proxy for question difficulty.
supporting_evidence: Authors explicitly state: 'we assume that the number of required skills corresponds to the difficulty of a question.'
Citation to Sugawara et al. (2017) supporting relation between skills and difficulty.
identified_assumptions.risk_if_unmet: If skill-count does not correlate with actual human or system difficulty, conclusions about dataset difficulty, cross-dataset comparisons, and recommendations for curriculum learning may be invalid or misleading.

identified_assumptions.assumption_text: The 13 defined skills cover the prerequisite phenomena needed across the evaluated RC datasets.

identified_assumptions.risk_if_unmet: Important reasoning types could be omitted or conflated, biasing frequency counts, undermining comparisons across datasets, and limiting utility of released annotations.

identified_assumptions.assumption_text: Annotators can reliably identify sentences 'needed' to answer a question across varied dataset contexts and task formats.
identified_assumptions.section_anchor: Section 4.1 Annotation Procedure; Section 6 (Competence of selecting necessary sentences)
supporting_evidence: Annotation protocol: annotators selected sentences and labeled skills; inter-annotator agreement reported.
Table 6 reports average number and distance of selected sentences per dataset.
identified_assumptions.risk_if_unmet: Inconsistent sentence selection could lead to inconsistent skill labeling and misestimation of how questions depend on context, affecting readability calculations (applied only to selected sentences) and downstream analyses.

identified_assumptions.assumption_text: Readability metrics designed for human reading (Vajjala & Meurers features, Flesch–Kincaid) appropriately reflect 'text ease of processing' relevant to RC tasks and to the selected sentences.
supporting_evidence: Authors select top features from Vajjala and Meurers (2012) and apply them to sentences selected during annotation; note that such metrics are for human readability and may not correlate with system performance.
identified_assumptions.risk_if_unmet: If these readability metrics do not align with what makes texts easy/difficult for the RC task (for humans or systems), then observed weak correlations may be due to metric mismatch rather than true independence between reading difficulty and question difficulty.

identified_assumptions.assumption_text: Sampling 100 questions per dataset (from development or gold sets) yields representative estimates of dataset-level properties.
identified_assumptions.section_anchor: Section 4.2 Dataset Specifications; Appendix A (sampling methods)

supporting_evidence: Authors report Pearson correlation coefficients between number of skills and readability features (Table 5).
identified_assumptions.risk_if_unmet: Non-linear or categorical relationships could be missed; reported low Pearson coefficients might understate other forms of association.

identified_assumptions.assumption_text: Aggregating different skill labels into a simple count (unweighted sum) is informative despite heterogeneity in skill complexity and overlap.
identified_assumptions.section_anchor: Section 3.1; Section 5 (number of required prerequisite skills; Table 3)
supporting_evidence: Table 3 reports frequency distribution of the number of required skills per question and uses average skill counts to compare datasets.
identified_assumptions.risk_if_unmet: Treating all skills equally may over- or under-state actual difficulty; some skills (e.g., logical reasoning) might be more demanding than others (e.g., punctuation), so counts may misrepresent comparative difficulty.

identified_assumptions.assumption_text: Nonsense/unsolvable questions are identifiable and separable from solvable questions by annotators.
supporting_evidence: Annotation instructions allowed annotators to select 'nonsense' for unsolvable questions; Table 2 reports nonsense frequencies per dataset.

identified_assumptions.risk_if_unmet: Inconsistent identification of nonsense questions can bias dataset difficulty estimates and inflate perceived gaps between readability and skill requirements.

specialist_reviews.analytical_summary: The manuscript advances an empirical analysis framework that combines a refined 13-item prerequisite-skill taxonomy with established readability metrics to characterize six RC datasets. The core reasoning chain is: (1) reading comprehension difficulty decomposes into (a) skills required to answer and (b) ease of reading; (2) we can operationalize (a) by annotating required prerequisite skills (counting them as a difficulty proxy) and (b) by applying human-centered readability features to sentences needed to answer; (3) by sampling 100 questions per dataset and annotating sentences+skills, we observe dataset-level distributions and compute correlations between skill-count and readability; (4) the observed weak correlations imply that readability and question difficulty are complementary and can be decoupled (e.g., easy-to-read but hard-to-answer datasets exist). The paper generally maintains internal continuity (motivation → metric design → annotation → descriptive analyses). However, several inferential links are assumed rather than empirically validated (notably the skill-count → difficulty link and representativeness of 100-sample draws). Some methodological choices (unweighted skill counting, use of Pearson r only, computing readability on annotator-selected sentences) create interpretive fragility that weakens claims that generalize to system performance or dataset construction recommendations.
logical_argument_graph: Node A: RC difficulty has two separable components: ability to read text (readability) and ability to answer questions (prerequisite skills).
Edge A→B: Psychological theory (McNamara & Magliano; Kintsch) supports decomposing comprehension into surface/textbase/situation-model and types of inferences (bridging/elaboration).
Node B: Operationalize readability via Vajjala & Meurers top features (lexical, syntactic, Coleman–Liau).
Node C: Operationalize question-difficulty via a taxonomy of prerequisite skills (refined to 13 skills).
Edge C→D: Assumption: number of required skills (skill-count) is a proxy for question difficulty (cites Sugawara et al.).
Node D: Annotation procedure — annotators select sentences needed to answer and label which of 13 skills are required (multi-label).
Edge D→E: Compute dataset-level aggregates: per-skill frequencies, distribution of number-of-skills per question, readability stats on selected sentences, sentence-distance metrics.
Node E: Statistical summary and correlation analysis across six datasets (100 sampled questions each).
Edge E→F: Empirical finding: low-to-moderate Pearson correlations (0.025 to 0.416) between readability and skill-count.
Node F: Interpretation: readability and question-difficulty are at best weakly correlated; they provide complementary views for dataset characterization and dataset/system design.
Edge F→G: Practical recommendation: use both metrics to guide dataset construction and curriculum-style system development (easy-read/easy-answer → easy-read/hard-answer → hard-read/hard-answer).

strengths.title: Clear theoretical motivation linking psychology and NLP
strengths.description: The paper grounds the two-metric approach in established cognitive theories (Kintsch; McNamara & Magliano) and textual-entailment literature, creating a principled rationale for separating readability and inference-skill dimensions.
evidence: Sections 1–2 cite McNamara & Magliano (2009), Kintsch (1988,1993), and Dagan et al. (2013) to link theoretical constructs to operational metrics.

strengths.title: Concrete operationalization and resource creation
strengths.description: Provides a reproducible annotation protocol, a refined 13-skill taxonomy, and produces dataset-level descriptive statistics across six diverse RC datasets.
evidence: Section 3.1 lists 13 skills with definitions; Section 4.1 describes annotation steps; Tables 2–3 and Figures 3–4 present aggregated outcomes.

strengths.title: Empirical cross-dataset comparison highlighting nontrivial patterns
strengths.description: The analysis surfaces meaningful dataset-level divergences (e.g., QA4MRE highest skill demands; MS MARCO many low-skill questions and higher nonsense rates) and provides actionable observations for dataset designers.
evidence: Section 5 summarizing per-dataset skill frequencies, nonsense rates, and readability contrasts (Table 2, Table 3, Table 4).

concerns.title: Skill-count used without empirical validation against difficulty
concerns.description: The central inferential step equates number-of-skills to question difficulty but provides no within-paper validation by correlating skill-count with human accuracy or system performance on the same sampled questions.
evidence: Assumption stated in Introduction referencing Sugawara et al.; no follow-up experiment comparing skill-count to performance metrics is presented.
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Add experiments correlating skill-count with human response accuracy/time and with multiple system performances on the same 100-item samples; alternatively present literature evidence quantifying the relationship or perform a targeted difficulty validation subset.

concerns.title: Limited inter-annotator agreement reporting
concerns.description: Reliability is reported only as a single aggregated percentage on a small sample (62 items) without per-skill agreement, kappa statistics, or confusion matrix, making it hard to assess taxonomy robustness.
evidence: Section 5 states 'The inter-annotator agreement was 90.1% for 62 randomly sampled questions.' No per-skill breakdown or statistical measure is provided.
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Report per-skill agreement (precision/recall or kappa), a confusion matrix for often-confused skills, and expand the adjudicated sample size; describe annotation instructions and training in detail (and attach labeling manual).

concerns.title: Representativeness of 100-question samples unclear
concerns.description: Sampling 100 items per dataset may underrepresent heterogeneous datasets (e.g., SQuAD, MS MARCO); results may be sensitive to sampling choices (paragraph vs article vs segment).
evidence: Section 4.2 and Appendix A outline sampling protocols (e.g., one paragraph per SQuAD article) but no analysis of sampling variance or sub-sampling stability is provided.
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Provide bootstrap or stratified re-sampling analyses showing stability of per-dataset metrics; justify sample size via power analysis or show consistency across multiple random seeds.

concerns.title: Readability measurement applied only to annotator-selected sentences
concerns.description: Computing readability on sentences chosen by annotators couples sentence-selection decisions with readability measures; if sentence selection is noisy or inconsistent, readability estimates may not reflect text-level ease-of-processing.
evidence: Section 3.2 states metrics are applied only to sentences that needed to be read; Section 6 acknowledges inability to evaluate sentence-selection competence.
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Report readability computed on (a) full context, (b) selected sentences, and (c) a fixed window around answer spans; compare results to show sensitivity and justify choice.

concerns.title: Correlation analysis limited to Pearson r and linear interpretation
concerns.description: The relationship between skill-count and readability may be non-linear or conditional on skill types; using Pearson correlation alone risks missing structured associations.
evidence: Section 5 reports Pearson coefficients between number of skills and readability metrics (Table 5) but does not present non-parametric tests or multivariate models.
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Augment analysis with Spearman rank correlations, logistic/ordinal regression predicting skill-count from readability features (and vice versa), and visualizations stratified by dataset and skill-type.

concerns.title: Unclear release and format of annotated resource
concerns.description: The paper asserts public release of annotations but provides no link, schema, or example file format, hindering reproducibility and reuse assessment.
evidence: Introduction and Conclusion state annotations 'will be publicly available' but no repository link or file description appears in main text.
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Include a link to the released annotations, a README summarizing fields and schema, and sample entries in the appendix or supplementary material.

specialist_reviews.analytical_summary: The manuscript proposes a two-class evaluation framework for reading comprehension (RC) datasets: (1) prerequisite skills (a refined 13-skill taxonomy) intended to capture the cognitive/inference operations required to answer RC questions, and (2) readability metrics (lexical, syntactic, traditional indices) applied to sentences judged necessary for answering. The authors annotate 100 randomly sampled questions from six RC datasets, report per-dataset skill frequencies, distribution of skill-count per question, readability scores (e.g., Flesch–Kincaid), and Pearson correlations between skill-count and readability. Core conclusions are that (a) the 13-skill taxonomy can be applied across diverse datasets with high aggregate inter-annotator agreement (90.1% on a 62-question sample), (b) skill-count is used as a proxy for question difficulty and datasets show differing profiles, and (c) there is only weak linear correlation between readability and number of required skills, implying readability and question difficulty are complementary and sometimes dissociated (e.g., MCTest easy-to-read but higher skill-count). The paper releases annotated labels for six datasets and discusses potential uses (dataset construction, curriculum learning).
logical_argument_graph: Premise: Human text comprehension can be usefully decomposed into 'strategic/skilled comprehension' (what inferences are required) and 'text ease of processing' (readability) (McNamara & Magliano 2009).

Step: Prior taxonomy (Sugawara et al. 2017) captures prerequisite skills but was limited; authors refine and extend to 13 skills grounded in textual entailment and psychology (Kintsch 1993, Dagan et al. 2013).

Operationalization: Annotators select sentences required to answer question and label which of the 13 skills are needed (allowing multiple labels); readability features (from Vajjala & Meurers 2012 and traditional indices) are computed on those selected sentences.
Assumption A1: Number of required skills (skill-count) is a proxy for question difficulty (citing Sugawara et al.).
Data: Randomly sample 100 questions per dataset across six RC datasets, annotate with three annotators; report aggregate IAA (90.1% on 62-question sample).
Analysis: Compute per-dataset skill frequencies, distribution of skill-count per question, readability metrics per dataset, and Pearson correlations between skill-count and readability metrics.

Observation: Correlations are generally low (0.025 to 0.416), datasets occupy distinct provinces (e.g., SQuAD high readability grade but low average skill-count), and nonsense/unsolvable questions vary by dataset.

Conclusion: Readability and prerequisite-skill requirements provide complementary information; skill-count may guide dataset construction and curriculum sequencing; annotations released for community use.

specialist_reviews.analytical_summary: The paper argues that reading-comprehension dataset quality should be characterized along two complementary axes: prerequisite cognitive/inference skills required to answer questions (a refined 13-skill taxonomy) and text readability (lexical/syntactic metrics drawn from prior readability work). The authors operationalize this by (1) defining the 13-skill taxonomy grounded in textual-entailment and psychology literature, (2) instructing annotators to mark sentences needed to answer and to label which skills are required, (3) computing readability features on the selected sentences, and (4) analyzing 100 randomly sampled questions from six RC datasets to compare skill distributions, skill-count (as a proxy for question difficulty), readability scores, and their correlations. The main empirical observation is a generally weak linear correlation between readability and skill-count across datasets, leading to practical recommendations: the two metrics are complementary for dataset diagnosis, and dataset sequencing (curriculum-style) can exploit their separation. The reasoning chain depends on key assumptions: that the 13 skills cover required phenomena, that annotators can reliably identify needed sentences and skills, and that simple skill-count is a valid proxy for difficulty. These assumptions are acknowledged but not fully validated within the study; consequently many conclusions are descriptive (taxonomy + dataset labels + observed correlations) rather than causal claims about model/human performance.
logical_argument_graph: Premise: RC difficulty is multi-faceted—reading text ease vs answering-question inference complexity (McNamara & Magliano 2009).

Operationalization: Have annotators select sentences necessary to answer and label which of the 13 skills apply; compute readability metrics on those sentences (Vajjala & Meurers features + Flesch–Kincaid).
Collect dataset samples (100 q per dataset × 6 datasets), compute skill frequencies, skill-count per question, readability scores, and Pearson correlations between skill-count and readability.

Observation: Weak to modest Pearson correlations across metrics/datasets (coeffs 0.025–0.416); dataset-level patterns show dissociation examples (e.g., MCTest easy-to-read but high skill-count; SQuAD hard-to-read but low skill-count).
Inference: Readability and prerequisite-skill characterizations provide complementary diagnostic views and can inform dataset construction and staged system development (curriculum learning).

Caveat: Many downstream prescriptive claims (e.g., using annotations for curriculum learning) rely on the unvalidated assumption that skill-count maps to human/system difficulty and on representativeness of sampled questions.
