Inter-annotator adjudication procedures and precise reliability metrics are not described; reproducibility of annotation decisions would benefit from examples and confusion matrices.

creativity_safeguard.novelty_not_validity_note: Although the elements (prerequisite-skill taxonomies, readability metrics, and dataset annotation) each have antecedents, their concrete combination into an applied two-axis diagnostic for multiple RC datasets and the specific 13-skill refinement represent an incremental but practical contribution; however, novelty here is about synthesis and resource provision, not a disruptive theoretical advance.
counterfactual_conditions_for_success: If skill-counts show robust correlation with human and model errors across multiple datasets, the taxonomy and annotations will be validated as useful difficulty proxies.
If per-skill inter-annotator agreement is high and confusion patterns are interpretable, the taxonomy will be reusable and reliable.
If readability features (or improved feature sets) can be shown to predict types of model failures, the two-axis diagnostic will directly inform system development and curriculum strategies.

novelty_lenses.rationale: The 13-skill taxonomy builds directly on Sugawara et al. and related textual entailment and psychology literature; the innovation is in reorganizing and adding fine-grained categories (e.g., ellipsis, meta-knowledge) and providing operational definitions for annotation.
evidence: Section 3.1 explicitly describes modifications/new skills and references prior taxonomies (Sugawara et al. 2017, Dagan et al.).
Applied annotations across six datasets show the taxonomy's practical applicability (Table 2).
uncertainty_flags: Per-skill reliability and boundary clarity are not reported, so practical reusability is not fully proven.

novelty_lenses.rationale: Analyzing six RC datasets with a unified protocol is a useful empirical extension over prior studies that analyzed fewer datasets, giving a broader comparative view though with moderate sample sizes.
evidence: Section 4 annotates 100 questions × 6 datasets and Section 5 reports cross-dataset patterns (Tables and Figures).
Paper contrasts automated vs crowdsourced datasets re: nonsense rates and skill distributions.
uncertainty_flags: Representativeness of 100-sample draws for large datasets is a concern; stratified or larger samples would strengthen claims.

novelty_lenses.verdict: moderately novel as a diagnostic tool
novelty_lenses.rationale: Combining cognitive/inference-skill labeling with readability feature analysis to produce actionable dataset characterizations is a pragmatic synthesis that can guide dataset construction and system training pipelines.
evidence: Discussion (Section 6) proposes curriculum learning and dataset sequencing based on the two axes; empirical plots show separable dataset positions (Figures 3–4).
uncertainty_flags: Empirical support that using this diagnostic improves system training or dataset design is not provided; effect on downstream tasks is speculative.

confidence_interval.rationale: Confidence reflects moderate-to-high certainty about the paper being an incremental, well-grounded contribution (taxonomy refinement + resource + multi-dataset descriptive analysis) but not disruptive; uncertainty stems from unvalidated assumptions (skill-count→difficulty), limited reliability reporting, and sampling choices.

prior_stage_inputs: RETRIEVED_LITERATURE_AND_GUIDELINE_CONTEXT (McNamara & Magliano 2009; Sugawara et al. 2017; Vajjala & Meurers 2012; Chen et al. 2016; Dagan et al. 2013; reviewer guidelines)
specialist_reviews.analytical_summary: The paper proposes a two-class evaluation frame for reading-comprehension (RC) datasets: (1) prerequisite/cognitive skills (a refined 13-skill taxonomy) and (2) readability (lexical/syntactic features drawn from Vajjala & Meurers and traditional indices). The authors operationalize the skills by an annotation protocol in which annotators (n=3) mark sentences necessary to answer a question and then mark which of the 13 skills are required (multiple labels allowed). They apply this to randomly sampled sets of 100 questions from six RC datasets (QA4MRE, MCTest, SQuAD, Who-did-What, MS MARCO, NewsQA), compute skill-frequency and skill-count statistics, compute readability on the selected sentences, and report descriptive comparisons and Pearson correlations between skill-count and readability metrics. Main empirical inference: there is only a weak linear correlation between readability and number of prerequisite skills, implying these metrics provide complementary views and that datasets can be easy-to-read but hard-to-answer and vice versa. The paper releases annotated labels (claimed), and suggests uses (dataset construction, curriculum learning). I treat the 13-skill taxonomy and the paired-metric framing as a potentially novel conceptual frame, but I explicitly separate the novelty signal from several methodological weaknesses (unvalidated skill-count→difficulty mapping, limited inter-annotator reporting, sampling and correlation-method choices). I flag specific places where the argument hinges on untested assumptions and suggest concrete validation steps that would preserve the innovative contribution if addressed.
logical_argument_graph: Premise: RC difficulty has at least two facets: comprehension of text (readability) and cognitive/inference operations needed to answer (prerequisite skills) (Section 1; McNamara & Magliano 2009).
Premise: Prior skill taxonomies are limited in scope or dataset coverage (Sugawara et al. 2017).
Method: Define/refine 13 prerequisite skills (Section 3.1) and select top readability metrics (Section 3.2).
Method: Annotation protocol — annotators select sentences needed, then mark skills (Section 4.1).
Data: Apply to 100-question samples from six datasets (Section 4.2; Appendix A).
Observation: Tabulate per-dataset skill frequencies, skill-count distributions, and readability scores (Tables 2–4; Figures 3–4).
Analysis: Compute Pearson correlations between skill-count and readability features (Table 5).
Result: Correlations weak (0.025–0.416) → interpret as weak linear relationship between readability and number of prerequisite skills (Section 5).
Conclusion: Readability and prerequisite-skills metrics provide complementary dataset characterizations; can inform dataset construction and curriculum-like system development (Section 6).

identified_claims.claim_text: A refined taxonomy of 13 prerequisite skills (reorganizing and extending prior work) can be used to annotate RC questions and characterize question difficulty.
evidence: Section 3.1 enumerates and defines 13 skills (Object tracking, Mathematical reasoning, Coreference resolution, Logical reasoning, Analogy, Causal relation, Spatiotemporal relation, Ellipsis, Bridging, Elaboration, Meta-knowledge, Schematic clause relation, Punctuation).
Annotation procedure (4.1) applied these skills across six datasets.
Table 2 reports frequencies (%) of these skills per dataset.
uncertainty_flags: Inter-annotator reliability reported only as a single 90.1% figure on 62 questions without per-skill agreement or confusion matrix.
No qualitative examples or annotation guideline snippets explain borderline distinctions (e.g., bridging vs. elaboration).
Possible subjective labeling boundaries not fully justified.

identified_claims.claim_label: Skill-count as proxy for question difficulty
identified_claims.claim_text: The number of required prerequisite skills corresponds to the difficulty of an RC question (i.e., more skills required → more difficult).
evidence: Explicit statement: 'we assume that the number of required skills corresponds to the difficulty of a question.'
Prior citation to Sugawara et al. (2017) which observed a relation between skills and difficulty.
uncertainty_flags: No validation within this manuscript linking skill-counts to human or system performance on the exact annotated questions.
Aggregate average skill-counts compared across datasets (Table 3) but not correlated with accuracy or response time measures.
Assumes equal weight for heterogeneous skills (no weighting or interaction modeling).

identified_claims.claim_text: Readability metrics (lexical, syntactic, traditional indices) and prerequisite-skill annotations together provide complementary views of dataset quality.
evidence: Readability metrics selected from Vajjala & Meurers (2012) and traditional indices (Figure 2; Section 3.2).
Comparative observations: SQuAD and QA4MRE high readability scores but differing skill profiles (Section 5).
Discussion suggests using both metrics jointly for dataset sequencing (Section 6).
uncertainty_flags: Complementarity supported descriptively; no multivariate model quantifies joint explanatory power or predictive utility.
Readability features were applied only to selected sentences (possible dependency on sentence-selection choices).

identified_claims.claim_label: Weak correlation between readability and skill-count
identified_claims.claim_text: Across six analyzed RC datasets there is only a weak correlation between text readability and number of prerequisite skills required to answer questions.
evidence: Reported Pearson correlations between skill-count and readability metrics range 0.025–0.416 (Section 5).
Figures 3–4 visualize dataset-level positions and question-level scatter for selected datasets.
uncertainty_flags: Correlation coefficients up to 0.416 could be meaningful in some contexts; manuscript labels them 'weak' without per-metric significance reporting.
Sampling (100 questions per dataset) may underpower detection of relationships, especially for large heterogeneous corpora.
Pearson correlation tests only linear associations; other relationships not explored.

identified_claims.claim_text: Datasets can be easy to read but contain difficult questions (MCTest), and conversely hard to read but easy to answer (SQuAD).
evidence: Figure 1 illustrative examples (SQuAD vs MCTest).
Section 5 narrative: 'MCTest is a good example of an RC dataset that is easy to read but difficult to answer.'; 'SQuAD was difficult to read ... but relatively easy to answer.'
Plots (Figures 3–4) show dataset separations.
uncertainty_flags: ‘Difficult to answer’ is inferred via skill-count rather than measured by human/system performance on the annotated questions.
Sampling and operationalization choices (selected sentences; paragraph sampling for SQuAD) may bias observed positions.

identified_claims.claim_text: Annotated labels and the two-metric framework can guide dataset construction and system development; annotations for six datasets are made publicly available.
evidence: Contribution 3: authors state annotations were made publicly available.
Section 6 suggests concrete uses (curriculum learning sequencing).
uncertainty_flags: No repository link, format description, or sample annotation dump included in the manuscript text.
No empirical test provided demonstrating that using these annotations improves dataset design or model training outcomes.

identified_claims.claim_label: Annotation protocol transferable across RC formats
identified_claims.claim_text: The annotation protocol (selecting sentences, then labeling skills) is equivalent across different RC task formulations (span, multiple-choice, cloze, multi-segment) for evaluating contextual entailments.
evidence: Section 4.1: annotators saw context+question+answer jointly and marked sentences and skills for all dataset types.
Paper states the procedure was applied across multiple datasets with differing formats.
uncertainty_flags: Authors acknowledge limitation: method cannot evaluate competence of searching for sentences or candidate answers.
Differences in dataset structure (e.g., MS MARCO multi-segment vs SQuAD paragraph) may influence annotator sentence-selection fidelity; per-dataset annotation variance not reported.

identified_claims.claim_text: Inter-annotator agreement on the prerequisite-skill annotation is 90.1% on a 62-question random sample.
evidence: Text: 'The inter-annotator agreement was 90.1% for 62 randomly sampled questions.'
uncertainty_flags: Agreement metric unspecified (percent exact match? Fleiss/Kappa? per-label F1?).
62-sample size small relative to 600 annotated questions; no per-skill breakdown or confusion matrix.

strengths.title: Coherent conceptual framing bridging cognition and NLP
strengths.description: The paper explicitly grounds its two-class metric choice in established cognitive theories (McNamara & Magliano; Kintsch) and prior entailment taxonomies, creating a theoretically informed evaluation frame.
evidence: Sections 1 and 2 cite McNamara & Magliano (2009) and Kintsch (1988, 1993) to justify the two classes.
Use of Dagan et al. (2013) and LoBue & Yates (2011) for entailment phenomena linkage.

strengths.title: Operationalization across diverse datasets
strengths.description: Applied the protocol to six heterogeneous RC datasets with different genres and formats, demonstrating feasibility of cross-dataset annotation.
evidence: Section 4.2 describes sampling and that 100 questions were annotated per dataset across QA4MRE, MCTest, SQuAD, WDW, MS MARCO, NewsQA.
Tables 2–3 and Figures 3–4 show cross-dataset summaries.

strengths.title: Practical, interpretable metrics useful for dataset diagnostics
strengths.description: The combination of skill frequencies, skill-count distributions, and readable readability indices yields interpretable summaries that can guide dataset curators.
evidence: Tables 2 and 3 present per-dataset skill frequencies and counts; Section 6 recommends curriculum-style dataset sequencing.

concerns.title: Unvalidated link: skill-count as proxy for difficulty
concerns.description: The central operational assumption that number of prerequisite skills equals question difficulty is asserted and relies on prior work but is not validated with human or model performance on the same annotated items in this paper.
evidence: Shared Analysis A1: 'we assume that the number of required skills corresponds to the difficulty of a question.'
No reported correlation or regression of skill-count against human accuracy, response time, or model performance on the same sampled questions.
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Measure skill-count correlation with human accuracy and with several model accuracies on the annotated 600 questions; report Spearman and logistic regressions (skill-count predicting success) and consider per-skill weights or interaction terms.

concerns.title: Insufficient inter-annotator reporting and per-skill reliability
concerns.description: Agreement is reported as a single overall percentage (90.1% on 62 items) without describing the metric, per-skill agreement, or common confusions—this obscures which skills are reliable versus subjective.
evidence: Shared Analysis: 'Inter-annotator agreement reported only for a 62-question sample (90.1%) — unclear how this generalizes.'
No confusion matrix or per-skill kappa/F1 presented.
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Provide per-skill agreement statistics (Cohen/Fleiss kappa or per-label F1), a confusion matrix for commonly conflated labels (e.g., bridging vs elaboration), and enlarge the adjudicated sample to at least 10–20% of full annotations.

concerns.title: Sampling representativeness and small sample per dataset
concerns.description: Using 100 randomly sampled questions per dataset is practical but may inadequately capture heterogeneity for large or multi-genre datasets (e.g., SQuAD, MS MARCO), affecting dataset-level inferences and correlation estimates.
evidence: Shared Analysis A5 notes 100-question sampling per dataset with sampling methods in Appendix A.
Large datasets like SQuAD contain diverse paragraphs; single-paragraph sampling may bias results.
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Report stratified sampling checks (topic, paragraph length, answer types) and perform sensitivity analyses with additional random seeds or increased sample sizes for large datasets; include bootstrap CI for correlation estimates.

concerns.title: Choice of linear correlation only (Pearson) may miss relationships
concerns.description: The paper relies on Pearson correlation to assess association between skill-count and readability; non-linear or rank-based relations may exist but are not explored.
evidence: Shared Analysis A6: Pearson correlation reported; no Spearman, Kendall, or multivariate analyses presented.
Authors describe correlations as 'weak' but without non-parametric confirmation or significance testing per coefficient.
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Complement Pearson with Spearman rank correlations, report p-values and CIs, test for non-linear patterns (e.g., LOWESS smoothing), and fit multivariate models including readability features jointly predicting skill-count or task success.

concerns.title: Readability features are human-centric; applicability to system difficulty unclear
concerns.description: Selected readability metrics originate from human second-language acquisition work and may not capture processing bottlenecks for contemporary RC models (e.g., transformer attention patterns).
evidence: Section 3.2: authors note these features are for human readability and may not correlate with system performance.
No experiments linking readability to model errors provided.
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Validate readability features against system error patterns across multiple models (e.g., BiDAF, BERT-based readers) and, if mismatch found, include model-centric difficulty features (e.g., lexical overlap, long-range dependency measures, named-entity ambiguity).

concerns.title: Taxonomy coverage and boundary justification
concerns.description: The paper refines prior taxonomies into 13 skills but provides limited empirical or qualitative justification for inclusion/exclusion decisions and for how these skills map onto cognitive operations or entailment phenomena.
evidence: Section 3.1 lists skills and mentions inspirations (Kintsch, Dagan et al.) but lacks worked examples tying each skill to annotated instances.
Shared Analysis: risk that some reasoning types are omitted or conflated.
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Provide illustrative example annotations for each skill (annotated text spans and rationale), a short decision tree/guideline for annotators, and rationale for why certain candidate skills were excluded or merged.

concerns.title: Annotation interface dependence: readability computed only on selected sentences
concerns.description: Readability metrics are calculated on sentences chosen by annotators as necessary to answer; this makes readability estimates dependent on sentence-selection behavior, which may vary and was not validated.
evidence: Section 3.2: 'We applied these metrics only to sentences that needed to be read to answer questions.'
Section 6: authors acknowledge they cannot evaluate competence of selecting sentences.
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Report analyses computing readability both on selected sentences and on full contexts (or on a standardized window) to assess sensitivity to selection decisions; measure inter-annotator agreement on sentence-selection.

concerns.title: Resource release transparency incomplete
concerns.description: The paper claims public release of annotations but provides no link, schema, or sample records in the manuscript, limiting reproducibility and reuse assessment.
evidence: Contribution 3: 'make the results publicly available' but no repository link in main text.
Shared Analysis: 'format, completeness, and accessibility details of released annotations are not shown.'
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Add a repository link (with DOI or stable URL), include README describing schema, license, and sample annotation files; optionally provide an author-verified preview in the appendix.

comparable_works.relevance: Direct antecedent taxonomy and empirical approach linking prerequisite skills to question difficulty.
comparable_works.similarity_or_difference: This paper extends Sugawara et al.'s skill taxonomy (from ~10 to 13 skills), applies it across more datasets, and reframes skills with entailment and cognitive theory.

comparable_works.relevance: Theoretical grounding for dividing comprehension into 'strategic/skilled comprehension' and 'text ease of processing'.
comparable_works.similarity_or_difference: Used by authors as conceptual justification for two metric classes; not directly compared empirically in RC context in prior NLP work.

comparable_works.relevance: Source of readability/linguistic feature selection.
comparable_works.similarity_or_difference: Authors adopted top features recommended by Vajjala & Meurers for human readability; difference: applied to sentences selected per question rather than entire texts or language-learning corpora.

comparable_works.relevance: Empirical cautionary precedent regarding dataset noise/unsolvable questions (CNN/Daily Mail).
comparable_works.similarity_or_difference: Used to justify sampling size and to motivate attention to nonsense/unsolvable question frequency; different focus from current paper's taxonomy.

comparable_works.relevance: Textual entailment taxonomy informing skill distinctions (bridging/elaboration).
comparable_works.similarity_or_difference: Authors cite Dagan et al. to align certain skills with entailment phenomena; current work operationalizes this linkage as part of taxonomy.

uncertainty_flags: Central assumption (skill-count→difficulty) is unvalidated within this manuscript.
Inter-annotator agreement summarized as a single percent on a small sample; no per-skill or confusion data.
Sampling 100 questions per dataset may not capture full heterogeneity; stratification checks absent.
Correlation analysis limited to Pearson coefficients; non-linear associations and statistical significance testing not shown.
Readability measures are human-focused; alignment with machine/system difficulty is untested.
alternative_interpretations: The weak correlation reported could arise from measurement mismatch: the readability indices (designed for human second-language acquisition) may fail to capture textual properties that drive the need for particular reasoning skills.

The observed dataset 'dissociations' (easy-to-read but hard-to-answer) may reflect annotation artifacts: annotators' propensity to mark multiple skills in narrative datasets versus encyclopedic text, rather than true task difficulty differences.
Skill-count may reflect question authoring style (complexity of the question formulation) more than underlying semantic difficulty of the answer retrieval/inference.
Non-linear relationships (e.g., readability affecting difficulty only beyond certain thresholds or interacting with specific skill types) could be present but missed by Pearson analysis.
transparency_notes: Please provide a public repository link, annotation schema, and sample records for the released annotations.
Report annotation instructions, examples for each skill, and adjudication/mediation process used for the 62-item agreement sample.
Provide per-skill agreement statistics (kappa or F1), confusion matrices, and number of items each annotator labeled.
Include p-values and confidence intervals for reported correlation coefficients and consider reporting Spearman coefficients and bootstrap CIs.

creativity_safeguard.novelty_not_validity_note: A sparse precedent for pairing a refined prerequisite-skill taxonomy with per-question sentence selection and sentence-level readability is not evidence of invalidity; rather it signals conceptual novelty. However, novelty must be disentangled from methodological gaps — i.e., the conceptual frame can be valuable even if the present empirical validation is incomplete.
counterfactual_conditions_for_success: If skill-counts correlate strongly with human and model error rates (after collecting those metrics on the same annotated items), then the taxonomy and the skill-count proxy will be validated as a useful difficulty signal.
If per-skill agreement is high for the majority of skills and common confusions are tractable (clear decision rules), the taxonomy will be reliable enough to support cross-dataset comparisons.
If multivariate models combining readability features and skill indicators predict human/model accuracy better than either alone, the two-class frame will demonstrate practical complementarity.
If the released annotations include clear examples and a decision guide, community reuse will refine and test the taxonomy across other RC formulations, amplifying its impact.

novelty_lenses.verdict: Potentially novel conceptual framing with promise
novelty_lenses.rationale: The explicit pairing of a refined, theory-grounded prerequisite-skill taxonomy with sentence-level readability applied to per-question selected sentences and cross-dataset annotation is not widely present in the literature; this framing foregrounds orthogonal axes of dataset difficulty and invites new dataset design and curriculum strategies.
evidence: Paper draws on cognitive theory (McNamara & Magliano) and entailment taxonomies but reorganizes skills and applies them across six datasets.
No close prior work retrieved that performs the same paired analysis at sentence granularity across multiple contemporary RC datasets.
uncertainty_flags: Novelty depends on empirical validation steps not present in paper (skill-count→difficulty, per-skill reliability).

novelty_lenses.verdict: Partially incremental in methods, but extends scope
novelty_lenses.rationale: Elements of the work build incrementally on Sugawara et al. (2017) and readability feature literature (Vajjala & Meurers 2012); the added value is breadth (six datasets) and reframing with cognitive theory rather than purely novel algorithmic advances.
evidence: Authors explicitly cite and extend Sugawara's taxonomy; readability metrics selection follows Vajjala & Meurers.
The analyses are descriptive summaries and correlation calculations rather than new predictive models.
uncertainty_flags: Extent of extension depends on how much the taxonomy revision changes annotations and whether released data enables novel downstream work.

confidence_interval.rationale: I am moderately confident (interval reflects uncertainty) that the conceptual pairing of prerequisite skills and readability is a useful and somewhat novel framing. Confidence is reduced by methodological gaps: unvalidated skill-count difficulty proxy, incomplete inter-annotator reporting, limited sampling and statistical analyses. If the authors address the listed methodological suggestions (validate skill-count against performance, report per-skill reliability, expand sampling/sensitivity checks, and release clear annotation artifacts), confidence in both novelty and utility would move toward the upper bound.

specialist_reviews.analytical_summary: The manuscript proposes a two-axis empirical framework for characterizing reading-comprehension (RC) datasets: (A) prerequisite skills (a refined 13-skill taxonomy, multiple-label annotations per question) and (B) readability (top lexical/syntactic features from Vajjala & Meurers plus traditional indices). The authors annotate 100 randomly sampled questions from six datasets and compute per-dataset skill frequencies, distribution of skill-count per question (used as a proxy for question difficulty), readability scores computed on annotator-selected sentences, and Pearson correlations between skill-count and readability. Main empirical claim: the linear correlation between number of required prerequisite skills and readability is weak (Pearson r range ~0.025–0.416), so readability and inferred question difficulty are largely complementary and can be dissociated (e.g., MCTest easy-to-read but higher skill-count; SQuAD reverse). The paper releases annotated labels (claimed) and frames possible uses (dataset diagnostics, curriculum learning). Key inferential vulnerabilities: the central mapping from skill-count to difficulty is assumed rather than validated against human or system performance on the same items; inter-annotator reliability is reported only as one aggregate percent on a small sample (62 items) without per-skill or chance-adjusted statistics; sampling (100 items per dataset) and the choice to compute readability on annotator-selected sentences introduce representativeness and measurement-dependence risks; correlation analysis is limited to Pearson r and may miss non-linear or conditional associations. I mark which claims are supported by manuscript evidence, which are partially supported, and where authors overstate by extrapolating beyond observed evidence.
logical_argument_graph: Premise: Human text comprehension decomposes into 'skills required to answer' and 'text ease of processing' (McNamara & Magliano 2009; Kintsch).
Define A: Refined 13 prerequisite skills (operational definitions) derived from prior taxonomies (Sugawara et al., Dagan et al., Kintsch).
Define B: Readability metrics (lexical/syntactic/traditional) chosen from Vajjala & Meurers and standard indices; applied to sentences marked as necessary by annotators.

Method: Sample 100 questions per dataset, three annotators select necessary sentences and label skills (multi-label), compute readability features on selected sentences, count number of skills per question.
Assumption: Skill-count (unweighted) maps to question difficulty (citing Sugawara et al. 2017).
Observation: Report per-dataset skill frequencies, average skill-counts, readability scores; inter-annotator agreement reported 90.1% on 62-item sample.
Analysis: Pearson correlations between skill-count and readability features yield low-to-moderate coefficients (0.025–0.416).

Conclusion drawn: Readability and prerequisite-skill-derived difficulty are weakly correlated, thus complementary; datasets can be easy-to-read but hard-to-answer and vice versa; annotations released can guide dataset construction and curriculum learning.

identified_claims.claim_text: A refined taxonomy of 13 prerequisite skills (reorganizing and extending prior work) can be used to annotate RC questions and characterize question difficulty.
evidence: Section 3.1 lists and defines 13 prerequisite skills with motivation tied to textual entailment and psychology.
Section 4.1 describes an annotation procedure applying these skills across six datasets.
Table 2 presents frequency distributions of the 13 skills across datasets.
uncertainty_flags: Inter-annotator reliability reported only as aggregate 90.1% on 62 items; no per-skill agreement or confusion matrices provided.
Some skills (e.g., bridging vs elaboration) have conceptual overlap and may be subjective in boundary cases.
Authors note practical annotation issues (e.g., 'none of the above' questions in QA4MRE) that taxonomy did not easily capture.

identified_claims.claim_label: Skill-count as proxy for question difficulty
identified_claims.claim_text: The number of required prerequisite skills corresponds to the difficulty of an RC question (i.e., more skills required → more difficult).
evidence: Explicit statement: 'From this observation, we assume that the number of required skills corresponds to the difficulty of a question.'
Citation to Sugawara et al. (2017) who observed a relation between required skills and difficulty.
uncertainty_flags: No empirical validation in this manuscript linking skill-count to either human reading difficulty (time/error) or system performance on the same annotated questions.
Skill-count treats all skills equally (unweighted), ignoring heterogeneity in intrinsic complexity.
Possible annotation artefacts: some labels may reflect annotator interpretation or sentence-selection choices, not intrinsic question difficulty.

identified_claims.claim_text: Readability metrics (lexical, syntactic, traditional indices) and prerequisite-skill annotations together provide complementary views of dataset quality.
evidence: Authors compute readability metrics on annotator-selected sentences and skill annotations; present contrasting dataset profiles (Tables 2–4, Figures 3–4).
Discussion (Section 6) describes how different datasets occupy different regions along readability and skill-count axes.
uncertainty_flags: Complementarity is shown descriptively but not quantitatively (no joint models or variance-partitioning to demonstrate independent explanatory power).
Readability metrics are human-centered; their interpretive link to system difficulty or human cognitive load is not tested here.

identified_claims.claim_label: Weak correlation between readability and skill-count
identified_claims.claim_text: Across six analyzed RC datasets there is only a weak correlation between text readability and number of prerequisite skills required to answer questions.
evidence: Table 5 reports Pearson correlations between number of skills and readability features with coefficients reported between 0.025 and 0.416.
Figures 3 and 4 visualize dataset- and question-level distributions showing dissociation for some datasets (e.g., SQuAD vs MCTest).
uncertainty_flags: 'Weak' is stated generally though some coefficients approach ~0.4; significance levels and per-dataset coefficient magnitudes are not fully reported.
Analysis used Pearson correlation only—linear association assumption; non-linear or conditional relationships not explored.
Sampling (100 items per dataset) may underrepresent heterogeneous corpora; chosen subset methods vary per dataset (Appendix A).

identified_claims.claim_text: It is possible to produce datasets that are easy to read but contain difficult questions (e.g., MCTest), and conversely datasets that are hard to read but easy to answer (e.g., SQuAD).
identified_claims.section_anchor: Introduction examples; Section 5 summary observations; Figures 3–4
evidence: Figure 3 places MCTest low on Flesch–Kincaid but relatively higher on average skill-count; SQuAD is higher on FK grade level but lower average skill-count.
Section 5 textual discussion highlights MCTest and SQuAD as exemplars of the dissociation.
uncertainty_flags: The designation of 'difficult to answer' relies on skill-count proxy rather than direct evaluation using human/system accuracy or response time.
Sampling procedures (e.g., selecting paragraphs/segments) and small sample size may influence the observed separation.

identified_claims.claim_text: Annotated labels and the two-metric framework can guide dataset construction and system development (e.g., curriculum learning stages); annotations for six datasets are made publicly available.
evidence: Authors state they 'make the results publicly available' and discuss potential uses (curriculum learning, dataset construction).
Methodology and metrics are described sufficiently to reuse if resources are available.
uncertainty_flags: No link, data format, or access particulars are provided in the manuscript or main text; resource accessibility and completeness are unverified here.
Utility for curriculum learning is speculative—no empirical tests or ablation experiments are provided to show that ordering by these metrics benefits learning.

identified_claims.claim_label: Annotation procedure equivalence across task formulations
identified_claims.claim_text: The annotation protocol (select sentences needed to answer, then label prerequisite skills) is equivalent across different RC task formulations (span, multiple-choice, cloze, multi-segment) for evaluating contextual entailments.
evidence: Section 4.1: annotators saw context, question, and answer jointly across tasks, selected sentences and applied skill labels.
Authors argue this makes annotations comparable across task formulations.
uncertainty_flags: Authors acknowledge the procedure cannot evaluate competence in finding answer candidates and that dataset format differences (e.g., MS MARCO segments) might affect annotation fidelity.
No inter-format diagnostics are provided to confirm consistent application of sentence-selection and labeling rules.

identified_claims.claim_text: Inter-annotator agreement on the prerequisite-skill annotation is 90.1% on a 62-question random sample.
evidence: Direct statement: 'The inter-annotator agreement was 90.1% for 62 randomly sampled questions.'
uncertainty_flags: Agreement reported as a single percentage without specifying metric (percent exact match vs. chance-adjusted kappa) or per-skill rates/confusion matrices.
62-question sample is small relative to total annotated items (600) and may not represent disagreement patterns across datasets and skills.

strengths.title: Clear, theoretically grounded two-axis framing
strengths.description: Links well-established psychological constructs (construction-integration, bridging vs elaboration) to operational metrics for RC dataset analysis.
evidence: Introduction connects McNamara & Magliano and Kintsch to the two classes of metrics.
Section 3 articulates mapping from cognitive theory to the 13-skill taxonomy and readability features.

strengths.title: Concrete operationalization and cross-dataset application
strengths.description: Provides explicit annotation procedure, applies it across six diverse RC datasets, and reports per-dataset descriptive statistics.
evidence: Section 4.1 details the annotation protocol used by three annotators.
Tables 2–3 and Figures 3–4 show results across QA4MRE, MCTest, SQuAD, Who-did-What, MS MARCO, and NewsQA.

strengths.title: Resource-oriented contribution potential
strengths.description: Claims to release annotations that could be reused for dataset diagnostics and further studies.
evidence: Contribution statement: 'We annotate six existing RC datasets ... and make the results publicly available.'
Method details are sufficient for replication if data are provided.

strengths.title: Descriptive insight: reading-difficulty and question-difficulty dissociation
strengths.description: Empirically demonstrates descriptive cases where readability and required inferential skills diverge across datasets.
evidence: Figures 3–4 and discussion highlight MCTest vs SQuAD separation.
Table 3 shows average skill-counts that vary independently from readability ranks in Table 4.

concerns.title: Skill-count used as unvalidated proxy for question difficulty
concerns.description: The manuscript assumes that the number of prerequisite skills (unweighted) corresponds to question difficulty but provides no direct validation against human error/time measures or system performance on the same annotated items.
evidence: Introduction: 'From this observation, we assume that the number of required skills corresponds to the difficulty of a question.'
No experimental section measuring correlation between skill-count and human accuracy/time or model performance is present in manuscript.
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Add empirical validation: measure human response times/error rates and/or system accuracies on the annotated 600 items and report correlations/ predictive models between skill-count (and per-skill presence) and observed difficulty; consider weighted skill models learned from data.

concerns.title: Insufficient inter-annotator reliability reporting
concerns.description: Inter-annotator agreement is summarized as a single 90.1% on 62 items without specifying the agreement metric, per-skill rates, or confusion patterns, limiting trust in label quality.
evidence: Section 5: 'The inter-annotator agreement was 90.1% for 62 randomly sampled questions.'
No kappa, per-skill F1, or confusion matrices presented.
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Report agreement using chance-adjusted statistics (Cohen's/Fleiss' kappa), per-skill precision/recall/F1, and a confusion matrix for common label confusions; increase annotation overlap beyond 62 items or provide stratified agreement analyses by dataset.

concerns.title: Sampling representativeness and sample size concerns
concerns.description: Using 100 randomly sampled questions per dataset (with differing selection rules across datasets) risks non-representative characterization for large, heterogeneous corpora like SQuAD and MS MARCO.
evidence: Section 4.2: 'We randomly selected 100 questions from each dataset' with Appendix A describing differing sampling methods (paragraph-level for SQuAD, segment selection for MS MARCO).
Acknowledgement in shared analysis that 100 may be insufficient for large datasets.
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Provide justification via sampling diagnostics: confidence intervals for key statistics; stratified sampling by article/topic/paragraph length; sensitivity analysis showing how results change with alternative samples or larger annotation subsets.

concerns.title: Readability computed on annotator-selected sentences introduces dependency
concerns.description: Readability features are computed on sentences annotated as 'needed to answer', which couples readability measures to annotator sentence-selection behavior and may confound dataset-level readability characterization.
evidence: Section 3.2: 'We applied these metrics only to sentences that needed to be read to answer questions.'
Table 6 reports average number and distance of selected sentences differing by dataset.
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Report readability both on selected sentences and on full context passages (or multiple granularities) to separate annotator selection effects from intrinsic text difficulty; analyze how selection length/distance correlates with readability metrics.

concerns.title: Correlation analysis limited to Pearson r and linear associations
concerns.description: The manuscript reports Pearson correlations only; non-linear relationships, conditional dependencies, or multivariate explanations (readability features jointly explaining skill presence) are not explored.
evidence: Section 5: Table 5 presents Pearson correlation coefficients between number of skills and readability metrics; no non-parametric or multivariate analyses shown.
Authors state coefficients range 0.025–0.416 but do not report significance or confidence intervals.
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Augment analysis with non-parametric correlations (Spearman), regression or classification models (e.g., predict skill-count from readability features using GLM or tree-based models) with cross-validation, and report effect sizes and p-values or bootstrap CIs; test for non-linear patterns.

concerns.title: Lack of per-skill analysis and weighting
concerns.description: Treating all skills equally in a simple count may obscure that some skills are inherently more demanding and differentially predictive of difficulty.
evidence: Taxonomy includes heterogeneous items (punctuation, coreference, logical reasoning, elaboration).
No weighting scheme or per-skill difficulty modeling presented.
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Report per-skill difficulty proxies (e.g., average system/human error when a skill is present), or learn weights via regression predicting human/system difficulty; include analyses of common multi-skill interactions.

concerns.title: Resource availability and reproducibility details missing
concerns.description: The manuscript claims public release of annotations but provides no link, license, file format, or documentation summary in the main text.
evidence: Contribution 3 statement claims public availability; no URL or access details in manuscript main body.
No appendix with data schema or annotation interface snapshots.
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Include a URL to the released dataset, describe file formats and column meanings, provide annotation guidelines and interface screenshots, and state licensing and citation instructions.

comparable_works.relevance: Direct antecedent: prior taxonomy and observation that more skills relate to higher difficulty.
comparable_works.similarity_or_difference: This paper builds on Sugawara et al.'s observation but expands to 13 skills and applies cross-dataset annotation; however, the present manuscript does not empirically re-validate the skill→difficulty link beyond referencing Sugawara.
comparable_works.source_trace: References and Section 3.1; cited in Introduction

comparable_works.relevance: Source of readability features used.
comparable_works.similarity_or_difference: Authors adopt the top features from Vajjala & Meurers for human readability; apply them to annotated sentences rather than whole documents.

comparable_works.relevance: Prior dataset analysis showing dataset-level quality issues and used to justify sampling size.
comparable_works.similarity_or_difference: Used as precedent for 100-item sampling but Chen et al. also performed deeper dataset diagnostics and highlighted unsolvable questions—an analogous concern here.

comparable_works.relevance: Readability/discourse measures alternative considered by authors.
comparable_works.similarity_or_difference: Authors note Pitler & Nenkova more suited for text quality but lacked discourse annotations; they instead used Vajjala & Meurers features.

uncertainty_flags: Central assumption A1 (skill-count → difficulty) is unvalidated within this manuscript; many interpretive claims depend on it.
Inter-annotator agreement is underreported (single aggregate percent; small overlap sample).
Sampling 100 items per dataset may not represent full dataset heterogeneity, especially for SQuAD and MS MARCO.
Readability metrics are human-centric; their relevance to machine understanding or actual human-in-the-loop difficulty for the annotated questions is untested.
Correlation analysis uses Pearson r only; non-linear and multivariate relationships unexplored.
alternative_interpretations: Low Pearson correlations could reflect metric mismatch (readability features not predictive of the inferential operations required) rather than true independence between reading ease and inference difficulty.
Annotated skill counts might reflect annotator behaviour or sentence-selection heuristics (e.g., conservative vs liberal marking) rather than intrinsic question complexity.

Some datasets' sampling methods (e.g., paragraph-level selection for SQuAD) could bias readability upward or downward, producing apparent dissociation that would disappear under stratified or exhaustive sampling.

Higher per-question skill-count might represent annotation granularity choices (splitting a complex inference into multiple labels) rather than additive cognitive load; alternative aggregation (weighted or hierarchical) might change cross-dataset rankings.
transparency_notes: Inter-annotator agreement should be decomposed by skill and reported with chance-adjusted measures (kappa) and confusion matrices.
Provide the release link and data schema in the main manuscript or appendix to verify reproducibility.
Report statistical significance (p-values or bootstrap CIs) for reported correlations and visualize distributions of both readability and skill-count at item level per dataset.
Document annotation instructions and examples for ambiguous edge cases (bridging vs elaboration, ellipsis vs omission) to aid re-use and replication.

creativity_safeguard.novelty_not_validity_note: The paired framing (prerequisite-skill taxonomy combined with readability metrics applied to annotator-selected sentences across multiple RC datasets) has limited direct precedent and therefore represents a meaningful conceptual contribution; novelty should not be conflated with empirical validity, which hinges on the unvalidated skill-count→difficulty mapping and limited reliability reporting.
counterfactual_conditions_for_success: If skill-count is empirically shown to correlate with human/system difficulty (via accuracy, response time, or learning curves), the taxonomy and dataset annotations become a powerful diagnostic resource.
If inter-annotator agreement per skill is high and confusions are small, the taxonomy will be robust and reusable across datasets.

If readability metrics computed on full contexts and on selected sentences yield similar patterns, the dependency on annotator selection will be minimal and conclusions about complementarity strengthened.

If multivariate models show that readability features and skill-presence jointly and independently explain variance in human/system difficulty, the complementary claim will be quantitatively validated.

novelty_lenses.lens: Incremental framing (builds on prior taxonomies and readability features)
novelty_lenses.rationale: The work refines an existing skills taxonomy (Sugawara et al.) and applies well-known readability features; the combination across six datasets and claimed public annotations are useful extensions rather than paradigm shifts.
evidence: Explicit refinement of Sugawara's skills to 13 items and adoption of Vajjala & Meurers features (Sections 3.1–3.2).
uncertainty_flags: Utility depends on annotation reliability and validation of skill-count as a difficulty proxy.

novelty_lenses.lens: Disruptive framing (introduces a two-axis diagnostic for dataset design and curriculum learning)
novelty_lenses.rationale: The conceptual separation of reading ease and inferential-skill complexity as design axes for dataset sequencing and curriculum learning is an instructive lens that could change how datasets are diagnosed and combined for training regimes, but practical impact requires empirical validation.
evidence: Section 6 proposes staging datasets by readability and skill difficulty for curriculum learning.
uncertainty_flags: No experiments demonstrating that ordering by these metrics improves model learning; resource release details missing.

confidence_interval.rationale: I provide probabilistic confidence only about the presence of the issues and evidence in the manuscript (high confidence) and about the unvalidated mapping between skill-count and true difficulty (high risk). Because final judgment tasks (e.g., whether the contribution is sound for downstream use) require empirical validations not present here, a single interval for overall reliability would be misleading; thus a full [0,1] interval is used with detailed qualifiers above.

consensus_findings: The paper presents a coherent, theory-grounded two-axis framing for characterizing RC datasets: (A) prerequisite/inference skills (a refined 13-skill taxonomy) and (B) readability (lexical/syntactic/traditional indices).

The authors operationalized the taxonomy via an annotation protocol (annotators select sentences needed to answer and label applicable skills) and applied it to samples from six diverse RC datasets, producing descriptive per-dataset summaries (skill frequencies, skill-count distributions, nonsense rates) and readability statistics.

Descriptive results show dataset-level patterns and instances of dissociation between readability and inferred question difficulty (examples: MCTest vs SQuAD), and reported Pearson correlations between skill-count and readability features are generally low-to-moderate (reported range ~0.025–0.416).

The manuscript claims (and intends) to release annotated labels for community reuse; the approach is framed as a practical diagnostic potentially useful for dataset curation and curriculum-style training.
disagreements: Strength of evidence for using unweighted skill-count as a proxy for question difficulty: reviewers uniformly flag this as the critical inferential assumption but differ on severity — all treat it as an unvalidated assumption, with several calling it a major methodological gap that must be tested (reviewers_1/2/3/4/5), while some characterize it as a plausible but currently unproven heuristic (structure_analyst, novelty_assessors).

Adequacy of inter-annotator agreement reporting: all reviewers agree reporting is insufficient, but differ on how damaging that is to conclusions. Some see the single aggregated 90.1% on 62 items as a major reliability shortcoming requiring per-skill kappa/confusion matrices (methodology_auditor, claim_verifier), while others view it as an initial positive signal needing more detail rather than fatal (novelty_assessor_incremental).

Interpretation of correlation magnitudes: reviewers concur coefficients are not large, but differ in labeling them 'weak' vs 'potentially meaningful' (some note coefficients up to ~0.416 could be informative if significant). There is disagreement over whether lack of non-linear/multivariate tests materially alters the stated complementarity claim.

Novelty appraisal: reviewers acknowledge incremental roots (Sugawara et al., Vajjala & Meurers) but disagree on novelty significance — some treat the paired diagnostic as a practically useful synthesis (novelty_assessor_incremental), others see it as potentially conceptually novel but empirically unproven (novelty_assessor_disruptive).
uncertainty_hotspots: Skill-count validity: whether unweighted count of annotated prerequisite skills correlates with true task difficulty (human error rate, response time, or model error) on the same items — no within-paper validation provided.

Annotation reliability per skill: absence of per-skill agreement metrics, confusion matrices, and adjudication details leaves uncertainty about which skills are reliable and which are subjective (notably adjacent categories like 'bridging' vs 'elaboration').

Sampling representativeness: sampling 100 questions per dataset (with dataset-specific selection rules) may underrepresent heterogeneity in large/heterogeneous corpora (e.g., SQuAD, MS MARCO); stability of dataset-level summaries and correlations under alternative samplings is unknown.

Readability measurement dependency: readability features were computed on annotator-selected sentences only, coupling sentence-selection variability with readability estimates and introducing measurement-dependence that could bias correlations.

Statistical analysis scope: reliance on Pearson correlation (linear association) without reporting significance, confidence intervals, non-parametric tests, or multivariate analyses leaves open the possibility of missed non-linear or conditional relationships.
model_diversity_effects: Role-specific perspectives (structure_analyst vs methodology_auditor vs novelty_assessors vs claim_verifier) lead to different emphases: structural reviewers focus on logical coherence and chain-of-evidence (spotting assumed inferential links), methodological reviewers emphasize reproducibility and statistical robustness (IAA, sampling, significance testing), novelty reviewers weigh conceptual contribution and potential impact (paired diagnostic) while flagging empirical validation needs, and claim verifiers prioritize explicit evidence supporting each claim.

This diversity preserves controlled disagreement: all roles accept the descriptive resource contribution, but methodological and verification roles downgrade extrapolations to applied recommendations (e.g., curriculum learning) until the skill-count ↔ difficulty mapping and annotation reliability are validated.

Because the ensemble includes both conservative reproducibility-focused and innovation-focused perspectives, the synthesis highlights that the conceptual framing is promising but that empirical and reporting gaps are the primary barriers to practical adoption.
meta_review.editor_guidance: Maintain the authors' claims as conditional and request targeted revisions to tighten empirical support and transparency. In particular, require (or ask authors to address): (1) direct validation of the skill-count proxy: correlate skill-count (and per-skill presence) with human difficulty proxies (accuracy, response time) and with multiple baseline model performances on the same annotated items, reporting Spearman/Pearson coefficients, confidence intervals, and effect sizes; (2) comprehensive inter-annotator agreement reporting: present the agreement metric used, per-skill kappa or per-label F1, confusion matrices, and adjudication procedure; expand double-annotation coverage if feasible; (3) sampling robustness diagnostics: show stability of dataset-level statistics and correlations across multiple random seeds or via bootstrap/stratified sampling (or justify sample size more rigorously); (4) sensitivity analyses for readability computation: report readability computed on (a) annotator-selected sentences, (b) full contexts, and (c) a standardized local window, and show how results change; (5) augment correlation analysis with non-parametric tests (Spearman), statistical significance (p-values or bootstrap CIs), and simple multivariate models (regressions/classifiers) to probe conditional or non-linear relationships and compute joint explanatory power of readability and skill features; (6) include a clear, accessible release of annotations: repository link/DOI, schema, sample entries, annotation guidelines, and code to compute readability features. Frame requested textual revisions so that claims about complementarity and utility are explicitly qualified where validations are absent.
meta_review.author_guidance: To strengthen the manuscript and make the resource actionable, address the following evidence-based items: (1) Validate the key assumption: run analyses relating skill-count and specific skill presence to human performance (crowd/expert accuracy or response time) and to one or more model baselines on the same 600 annotated items; report correlation coefficients (Pearson and Spearman), logistic/ordinal regression results, and confidence intervals; if full validation is infeasible, clearly qualify claims and propose a concrete validation plan. (2) Expand and detail inter-annotator reliability: report the metric used, per-skill agreement (kappa or per-label F1), a confusion matrix highlighting common label confusions, and document the adjudication protocol; if some skills show low reliability, consider merging or clarifying definitions with examples. (3) Provide sampling and robustness analyses: show whether per-dataset summaries and correlations are stable across multiple random samples or stratified draws; include bootstrap confidence intervals for key statistics. (4) Decouple readability from annotator selection: compute readability on alternative units (full context, fixed windows) and report sensitivity; explain and justify the chosen granularity in relation to intended use. (5) Broaden statistical analyses: add Spearman correlations, report p-values/CI for coefficients, and fit simple multivariate models (e.g., GLM or random-forest) to assess joint explanatory power of readability features and skill indicators for predicted difficulty. (6) Release annotations and code with clear documentation: repository link/DOI, data schema, sample records, annotation manual with worked examples, and scripts to reproduce analyses and compute readability features. (7) Temper prescriptive recommendations (e.g., curriculum learning) or, if possible, provide an initial small-scale experiment showing utility (optional). Provide these additions in main text, supplemented by an appendix if length is an issue.
transparency_report: Annotation overlap and IAA reporting are limited in the main text: a single aggregate agreement figure (90.1% on 62 items) is provided without metric specification (percent exact match vs chance-adjusted measures) or per-skill breakdown; adjudication and annotator training materials are not included.

Sampling procedures are described in Appendix A but per-dataset sampling heterogeneity (paragraph vs segment selection) is present; no bootstrap or sensitivity diagnostics are reported to assess representativeness of 100-item samples.

Readability computation is performed on annotator-selected sentences only (explicit), but alternative units (full context or windows) and their results are not reported, making readability estimates dependent on annotation behavior.

Statistical reporting is limited: Pearson correlations are reported (range 0.025–0.416) but p-values, confidence intervals, non-parametric correlations, and multivariate models are absent from main results.

Resource release is asserted ('publicly available') but no repository link, schema, license, or sample files are presented in the main manuscript; hence reproducibility and immediate reuse are impeded.
epistemic_limits: This synthesis is bounded by the materials presented in the manuscript and reviewers' focus: we cannot observe the released annotation files, the annotation interface, or any supplementary experiments that may exist but were not included in the main text. Consequently, inferences about annotation quality, dataset representativeness, and practical utility of the taxonomy are conditional on the completeness of reporting. Key claims that depend on unvalidated assumptions (notably that unweighted skill-count maps to real difficulty for humans or models) remain epistemically uncertain until direct validation is provided. Statistical characterizations based on 100-item samples per dataset are informative but may not generalize to full dataset populations without sampling-robustness checks. Finally, absence of per-skill reliability metrics limits our ability to assess which parts of the taxonomy are stable versus subjective; any downstream use (e.g., curriculum learning) should treat the taxonomy and counts as provisional signals requiring empirical calibration.

human_facing_meta_review.summary: The manuscript proposes a two-axis framework to characterize reading-comprehension (RC) datasets: (1) prerequisite/inference skills (a refined 13-skill taxonomy) annotated per question, and (2) text readability (lexical/syntactic/traditional indices) computed on sentences judged necessary to answer. The authors annotate 100 randomly sampled questions from six RC datasets, report per-dataset skill frequencies, distributions of skill-count per question (used as a difficulty proxy), readability statistics, and Pearson correlations (reported range ≈ 0.025–0.416). They claim the two metrics are complementary (readability and inferred skill difficulty are weakly correlated), illustrate dissociations across datasets (e.g., MCTest vs SQuAD), and state that annotations will be publicly released to aid dataset curation and curriculum design.
strengths: Conceptual clarity: framing RC difficulty along two theoretically motivated axes (cognitive/inference skills vs text ease-of-processing) grounded in cognitive and entailment literature (e.g., McNamara & Magliano; Kintsch; Dagan et al.).

Operational contribution: a concrete 13-skill taxonomy with an explicit annotation workflow (select answer-relevant sentences, then multi-label skills) applied across six diverse RC datasets, producing descriptive cross-dataset comparisons.

Descriptive empirical signal: observed dataset-level patterns and illustrative dissociations (cases where readability and annotated skill-counts diverge) that are useful diagnostic insights for dataset designers.
limitations: Key inferential leap unvalidated: the central assumption that an unweighted count of annotated prerequisite skills maps to question difficulty is not empirically validated against human or system performance on the same annotated items; downstream claims (e.g., curriculum sequencing) rest on this untested mapping.

Incomplete annotation reliability reporting: inter-annotator agreement is summarized only as a single aggregated figure (90.1% on 62 items) without specifying the agreement metric, per-skill kappas or F1s, confusion matrices, or details of adjudication and annotator training—obscuring which skills are reliable versus ambiguous.

Sampling and representativeness: only 100 randomly sampled questions per dataset were annotated, with dataset-specific sampling rules (appendix). For large, heterogeneous corpora (e.g., SQuAD, MS MARCO) this may underrepresent internal variation and affect per-dataset summaries and correlations.

Readability measurement dependency: readability features are computed on annotator-selected sentences only, coupling readability estimates to sentence-selection behavior; without sensitivity analyses (readability on full context or fixed windows), measurement dependence may bias correlations and interpretations.
open_questions: Can the authors provide empirical validation linking skill-count (and/or presence of specific skills) to observed difficulty measures (human accuracy, response time, and/or model error) on the same annotated 600 items? Please report Pearson and Spearman correlations, regression coefficients, and confidence intervals.

Please report detailed inter-annotator reliability: which agreement statistic was used, per-skill kappas or per-label precision/recall/F1, a confusion matrix for commonly confused labels (e.g., 'bridging' vs 'elaboration'), and the adjudication protocol. If some skills show low reliability, how will taxonomy use be affected?

How sensitive are the dataset-level readability and skill-count summaries to sampling variance? Provide bootstrap or repeated-sampling estimates (or stratified sampling diagnostics) to show stability of reported correlations and dataset positions in the two-axis space.

How do readability estimates change when computed on (a) annotator-selected sentences, (b) full contexts/passages, and (c) fixed windows around answer spans? Please include these comparisons to demonstrate that readability results are not driven by sentence-selection artifacts.
consensus_snapshot: All reviewers agree the paper introduces a coherent, theory-grounded two-axis diagnostic (skills + readability) and provides a concrete annotation protocol and cross-dataset descriptive analyses.
All reviewers identify the unvalidated mapping from skill-count to actual difficulty and limited IAA reporting as the principal methodological gaps.
All reviewers consider the descriptive annotations and taxonomy to be a potentially useful resource if accompanied by fuller reliability, validation, and reproducibility details.
disagreement_snapshot: Degree of harm from current methodological gaps: some reviewers regard the unvalidated skill-count proxy and sparse IAA reporting as major flaws needing correction before claim generalization; others view them as addressable deficiencies that do not negate the descriptive resource value.

Interpretation of reported correlation magnitudes: while all note correlation coefficients are not large, reviewers differ on whether coefficients up to ~0.416 might be meaningful in context absent reported significance/CIs and non-linear analyses.
uncertainty_snapshot: Uncertainty whether skill-count meaningfully predicts human or model difficulty (skill-count ↔ difficulty remains an open empirical question).
Uncertainty about which specific skills in the 13-item taxonomy are reliable versus ambiguous due to lack of per-skill IAA and confusion data.
Uncertainty about generalizability of 100-item samples to full datasets and whether sampling idiosyncrasies drove observed dataset separations.
source_trace: Sugawara et al. (2017) — prior prerequisite-skill taxonomy and reported relation between number of skills and difficulty; used by authors to motivate skill-count proxy (manuscript cites Sugawara et al.).
Vajjala & Meurers (2012) — source of top lexical/syntactic readability features applied by the authors (Section 3.2).
McNamara & Magliano (2009); Kintsch (1988/1993) — cognitive-theory grounding for decomposing comprehension into text processing vs inferential operations (used in Introduction and Related Work).
Chen et al. (2016) — precedent for dataset-quality sampling considerations and noise diagnostics (referenced in sampling justification).
transparency_notes: The manuscript asserts public release of the annotated labels but does not include a repository URL, data schema, or sample records in the main text. Inter-annotator agreement is reported only as an aggregate percent (90.1% on 62 items) without metric specification, per-skill rates, or confusion matrices. Sampling procedures are described (Appendix A) but no bootstrap/robustness diagnostics or confidence intervals for reported correlations are provided. Readability is computed on annotator-selected sentences only; the manuscript does not report sensitivity analyses using full contexts or fixed windows. To improve transparency and reproducibility, include the annotation files (with README/schema), annotation guidelines and examples for each skill, per-skill IAA statistics, sampling scripts, and code used to compute readability features.
human_facing_meta_review.editor_guidance: Request revisions that focus on empirical validation and transparent reporting rather than asking for wholly new conceptual framing. Specifically, ask authors to: (1) empirically test the skill-count ↔ difficulty mapping on the annotated sample by correlating skill-count and per-skill presence with human accuracy/response-time and with multiple model baselines; (2) expand IAA reporting (specify metric, per-skill kappas or F1s, confusion matrices, and adjudication steps) and increase overlap if feasible; (3) provide sampling-robustness diagnostics (bootstrap or repeated-sample CIs) to assess stability of dataset-level statistics; (4) perform sensitivity analyses of readability computation (selected sentences vs full contexts vs fixed windows); (5) complement Pearson with Spearman/non-parametric tests, report p-values/CI, and include simple multivariate models probing joint explanatory power; (6) publish the annotations, schema, and code with documentation. Frame any publication-level claims to be conditional on these validations.
human_facing_meta_review.author_guidance: To strengthen evidence and utility, please: (1) Validate the central assumption by computing correlations/regressions between skill-count (and per-skill presence) and empirical difficulty—human accuracy/time and baseline model errors—on the same annotated items; report Pearson and Spearman correlations, regression coefficients, p-values, and confidence intervals. (2) Report detailed inter-annotator reliability: state the agreement metric used, provide per-skill kappas or per-label F1, a confusion matrix showing common confusions, and describe the adjudication/training procedures (attach guidelines and worked examples). If some skills show low reliability, discuss merging/clarification. (3) Show sampling robustness: present bootstrap or repeated-sampling estimates for key statistics and correlations, or justify sample size and sampling protocol more rigorously. (4) Decouple readability from sentence-selection: compute readability on full contexts and on fixed windows and compare results to those on selected sentences to show sensitivity. (5) Broaden statistical analysis beyond Pearson: include Spearman correlations, bootstrap CIs/p-values, and simple multivariate models (GLM or tree-based) to probe conditional and non-linear relationships and to quantify joint explanatory power. (6) Release data and code with a clear README, example entries, schema, and scripts used for analyses and feature extraction. (7) Temper prescriptive recommendations (e.g., curriculum learning) unless direct validation is provided, or present a small illustrative experiment if feasible.
human_facing_meta_review.comments:
Summary: The paper presents a useful, theory-grounded two-axis diagnostic for RC datasets—prerequisite skills (13-label taxonomy) and readability features—applied across six datasets with annotated samples. The descriptive findings (skill frequencies, skill-count distributions, and readability contrasts) and observed dissociations are informative.

Strengths: Conceptual clarity linking cognition and NLP; operationalized taxonomy and annotation workflow; multi-dataset empirical application producing interpretable diagnostic summaries.

Limitations: (1) The mapping from unweighted skill-count to question difficulty is not validated within the manuscript against human or model performance on the same items. (2) Inter-annotator reliability is underreported (single aggregate percent without per-skill metrics or confusion matrices). (3) 100-item per-dataset sampling may underrepresent heterogeneity; no bootstrap/stability analyses reported. (4) Readability is computed only on annotator-selected sentences, coupling measurement to annotator behavior without sensitivity checks.

Open Questions: (1) How well does skill-count (and specific skills) predict human/model difficulty on the annotated items—please provide correlation/regression results with CIs? (2) What are per-skill agreement statistics and common confusions; could some skills be merged or better defined? (3) How stable are dataset summaries across different random samples or stratified sampling? (4) How sensitive are readability-results to using full contexts or fixed windows rather than annotator-selected sentences?

Transparency: The manuscript claims a public release of annotations but lacks a repository link, schema, or sample files in the main text; inter-annotator protocol and per-skill reliability measures are not provided; statistical reporting omits p-values and confidence intervals and relies on Pearson correlations only. Providing annotation artifacts, IAA breakdowns, sampling scripts, and analysis code will materially improve reproducibility and community uptake.

confidence_interval.rationale: Lower bound reflects uncertainty due to the unvalidated skill-count↔difficulty assumption, incomplete IAA breakdown, and limited sampling diagnostics. Upper bound reflects confidence in the paper's concrete descriptive contributions (taxonomy, annotations, cross-dataset summaries) and the theoretical framing—these parts are well motivated and likely reproducible if the requested transparency and validation steps are addressed.

This is a composite score reflecting your assessment of soundness, excitement, and also other factors like novelty and impact.
